title: Shvetaketu and the ember
hookLine: a proud student is told to stop eating, and his father's lesson arrives as an ember
carry: the mind is made of food

lines: A STUDENT HOME, SURE OF HIMSELF.
WHAT A MEAL HAS TO DO WITH A MIND.
cards: A student comes home after years of study, sure of himself, full of verses. You met him back in year three, the proud one: Shvetaketu. His father, Uddalaka, decides to test him, and the test isn't a debate.
It's a diet. Eat nothing for a while, the father says. Drink all the water you like.
Then come back and recite what you know. The experiment sits in the sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad. Today, what a meal has to do with a mind.

teach.b: It starts with a claim, paraphrased. Food, once eaten, divides three ways. The coarsest part leaves the body.
The middle part becomes flesh. The finest part becomes mind.

teach.h: THE MIND, MY DEAR, IS MADE OF FOOD
teach.b: Uddalaka puts it in one line, in Sanskrit annamayam hi somya manah: the mind, my dear, is made of food. Water, he adds, becomes breath, and heat becomes speech. Then the test.
The text says fifteen days without food, with water allowed. Shvetaketu comes back, and his father asks for the verses. They don't come to me, sir, he says.
So Uddalaka gives him a picture.

teach.h: AN EMBER THE SIZE OF A FIREFLY
teach.b: A great fire has burned down to one ember, the size of a firefly. It can't burn much now. Add straw, and it blazes again.
Go and eat. Shvetaketu eats, comes back, and the verses are all there. And he understood, the text says.
Three things. First, it's humbling. The young scholar who thought learning lived somewhere above the body finds it leaning on lunch.
Second, it's kind to the body. Nobody is scolded for needing to eat; the plate is part of how a person thinks. Third, it's a doorway.

In this same chapter Uddalaka will say tat tvam asi, you are that: the self, atman, is one with the reality in everything. He's leading his son there, and food is one of the first things he reaches for.

teach.h: A TEACHING STORY, NOT A FASTING PLAN
teach.b: And plainly, since these days hold Ayurveda to a careful standard: this is a teaching story, not a fasting plan, and nobody should copy the experiment.
What it offers is a way to see a meal: not fuel poured in while the real you is somewhere else, but an ember being fed.

how: Some Hindus fast on particular days as a devotional practice, while teachers of the Upanishads read Uddalaka's experiment as a lesson about the self, not as a fasting rule.

o: a fast kept for days to sharpen the memory for verses
a meal seen as feeding the mind, like straw on an ember
a meal of pure foods only, eaten just before study

games.q: the meal, divided — tap the pairs.

s: in the Chandogya, Uddalaka says the mind is made of food
annamayam hi somya manah: the mind, my dear, is made of food.
Shvetaketu goes without water as well as food
his father tells him to drink as much water as he likes. only food is held back.
the story is a fasting plan to copy
it's a teaching story about what a self is. nobody should copy the experiment.

games.q: you're Uddalaka. your son has fasted, and now he can't recall the verses he learned. what do you do?
o: send him back to study them again.
tell him to go and eat, then ask again.
tell him the verses never mattered.
games.why: he gives him the ember, a coal the size of a firefly that blazes with straw, and sends him to eat. the verses come back, and Shvetaketu understands.

practice: Rest a hand low on the belly if you like, and let a small ember come to mind, glowing, about the size of a firefly.

With each breath in let it brighten a little, the way a coal brightens when air reaches it, and with each breath out let it settle and glow. If you pray, give thanks for the food that is holding you up right now.

wordCard.voice: Food as practice. In the Chandogya, the finest part of a meal becomes mind, and a hungry student's verses come back after he eats. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Chandogya Upanishad 6.5.4: the mind, my dear, is made of food. anna is food; manas is mind.

carryVoice: Your line: the mind is made of food. Feed the ember, the way Uddalaka sent his son to eat. Rest well.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.1–3 (Shvetaketu returns from study, proud)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.5.1–4 (food divides three ways; the mind is made of food, breath of water, speech of heat)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.7.1–6 (fifteen days without food, water allowed; the ember the size of a firefly; he eats and remembers)
